subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just one thing to say on this matter. We had an extensive and, I think, worth-while debate on it last week, but I have one further remark to make on third reading. It is this. There will be no solution to the problem of Canadian gold mining without an increase in the price of gold. This can be done by two methods, namely by allowing the price of gold to increase through the operation of the free market or by joint international action by edict or governmental decree. I would hope that the

former would be the method taken, because it is the economically correct method. As I have pointed out, gold is becoming extremely scarce in world trade. This is a world danger.
We have seen this country, Mr. Speaker, set an example with regard to the international bank for reconstruction. We have taken courageous action in making our initial payment to this organization available for the purposes of the bank. I suggest that the bank's actions with regard to international trade have been very helpful and very constructive. Having taken this initial action with regard to the international bank for reconstruction, we have just completely paid up our $65 million, making our subscription to this organization complete. We have taken courageous action in freeing our dollar and abolishing exchange control. We have not, however, taken similar courageous action with regard to the international monetary fund. Until we are prepared to take that necessary and desirable courageous action with regard to gold trading with the international monetary fund there can be no solution to the Canadian gold problem.
I further submit, Mr. Speaker, that had we been prepared to take that courageous and forthright action we should have met with the same degree of international approbation that our action with regard to the international bank for reconstruction has brought us.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO YEARS

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO YEARS
speechtext: I have no further statement to make on this bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO YEARS
speechtext:
I will take a moment, then, to express regret that the government has no statement to make on this vitally important question. We are still dealing with a great national problem on a temporary stopgap basis. The measure that is before the house, while it must be supported by us all as far as it goes, is nevertheless nothing more than a stopgap temporary measure. I hope that before long the government is going to come to grips with this problem, and really show that it is seized of the importance of the problem and is going to make some resolute effort to persuade the United States government to increase the price that it is paying for Canadian gold, and to seek also remedial action, through the international monetary fund, to relieve the Canadian gold mining industry of some of the shackles that have been imposed upon it

as a result of the decisions of the international monetary fund to which the government of this country has been a party.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ZONING OF AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Subsection 2 of the bill adds five subsections to section 4 of the Aeronautics Act. Some question has arisen concerning two of these new subsections. One, which is numbered 9 in this present bill, provided that an applicant for compensation for damage resulting from these airport zoning regulations must commence proceedings within one year from the time the zoning regulations were filed in the land registry or other appropriate office. When the bill was given consideration by the committee, that period was changed from one year to two years, which I think is a great improvement. We are not quarrelling with that particular subsection, now that that change has been made. But 55704-176
Aeronautics Act
we are still very much worried about the new subsection 8, which is the one providing for compensation for damage resulting from these airport zoning regulations. If hon. members will refer to the subsection in question they will find that it reads as follows:
Every person whose property is injuriously affected by the operation of a zoning regulation is entitled to recover from Her Majesty, as compensation, the amount, if any, by which the property was decreased in value by the enactment of the regulation, minus an amount equal to any increase in the value of the property that occurred after the claimant became the owner thereof and is attributable to the airport.
That means of course that a person who has suffered damage by reason of this zoning regulation having been passed can claim compensation for the decrease in value, but there has to be deducted from that compensation any increase in value of his or her property which occurred after he or she became owner of the property, and which is attributable to the airport. That would work out in this way. Suppose that damage caused by the zoning regulations amounts to $1,000. Then the owner of the property affected will not necessarily be entitled to get that sum of $1,000 from the crown, because the judge of the exchequer court, after determining that the damage is $1,000, would have to examine into other factors. First of all, he must decide whether the setting up of the airport in question increased the value of the property. Then he must decide whether the owner who is claiming the compensation got that property before or after the airport was built. If the property was acquired before the airport was built, and if there has been any increase in the value of his property by reason of the airport being built, then that amount of increase is deducted from the compensation. So that the owner of the property may very well find his thousand dollars wiped out completely by this string attached by the section with respect to the compensation. It should be pointed out that after this deduction has been made ini the damage payable because of the zoning regulations, then should the land itself be taken over by the government under the Exchequer Court Act, the same deduction can be made again. In other words, the increase in the value of the land by reason of the placing of the airport could be deducted from the amount a man would receive for his property. This would follow as a result of the provisions of section 50 of the Exchequer Court Act.
We believe this section is not properly worded. It is our feeling that, instead of deducting the amount by which the land was increased in value by reason of the airport, there should be deducted only such increase

Aeronautics Act
in value as is caused by the zoning regulations. Then an applicant who has proved that he has suffered damage would have deducted whatever increase in the value of the property resulted from the zoning regulations themselves, rather than mixing up the zoning regulations and the value of the property, as is done under the wording of the section as it now stands.
We suggest that the minister give further consideration to making a change accordingly in this subsection. The owner who is going to apply for compensation will have to go to the exchequer court, and that is an expensive procedure, as well as being cumbersome. I doubt whether many owners will be able even to get the compensation under this act to which they are entitled. It seems unfair that they should be handicapped by having the restriction contained in the last three lines of paragraph 8 in the bill, which reads-
-minus an amount equal to any increase in the value of the property that occurred after the claimant became the owner thereof and is attributable to the airport.

speechtext:
I should like to state my position concerning this paragraph. However, what I had intended to say has been covered by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and I have no desire to repeat what he has said.

I placed my views on record in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, but I think some further observations would be in order at this time. As the minister knows, in the bill which was to have come before the house on a previous occasion, the question of compensation had not been accepted by the government. Upon review, compensation was restored to the bill, with the result that the bill became more acceptable to many who had thought that the matter of compensation would raise difficulties in the minds of those who were adjoining owners of properties.
My thought concerning the paragraph at this time is that I fear that what has been done has been to give with one hand and to take away with the other. I am concerned because I feel this might mean that the compensation that was to become payable after adjudication by the exchequer court, by virtue of the express paragraph in the subsection, may amount to very little. Compensation is the chief feature of the bill as it relates to the adjoining owners of land. I am concerned particularly because all the rights and all the money values that could be awarded to an owner adjoining an airport may be subtracted as a result of the minus feature in the section.
I suggest that on this ground the bill is defective. In addition to that the question of ownership arises, because the section says that from whatever may be given by virtue of a decrease in value of land, due to these regulations, there may be subtracted an amount equal to any increase in the value of the property occurring after a claimant becomes its owner.
I pointed this out in committee, and I do so again at this time by way of emphasis to the minister, in the hope that at some future time a correction can be made. However, I should think that it is not at this time too late to make the change. It seems to me the provision in the paragraph does discriminate between the owner who held the property when the airport was first installed, and the new owner who has owned the property within recent months. Certainly they are not being treated in the same way in this paragraph, as I see it.
It seems to me that in the paragraph there is a vast difference between the way we treat the man who has held the land for a long time and the one who has acquired it only a short time ago. I do not wish to repeat in their entirety the observations I made in the standing committee, but I would point out to the minister that the wording

of the last two sentences in paragraph 8 is in my opinion faulty in that it indicates that such compensation shall be-
-minus an amount equal to any increase in the value ol the property that occurred after the claimant became the owner thereof and is attributable to the airport.
I had hoped the standing committee would see fit to support me. However, they did not see eye to eye with my view, with the result that I lost the battle. It is not -the first time I have lost a battle in the House of Commons, so I do not feel bad about it. I think it would have been better if we omitted the words, "is attributable directly to the airport." As the minister knows, in some of these instances the value of land has not been increased just because there happens to be an airport there. The increase may be attributable to the fact that there are large installations of industry and manufacturing at that particular point. I have in mind at the moment the Malton airport where the A. V. Roe Company have a large aircraft manufacturing centre. That fact has attributed to the increase in value of land about the airport much more, if I may say so, than has the airport itself.
I think that distinction should be drawn so that the "minus" provision would not be so broad as it might perhaps be interpreted to be. I think that would carry out the design which all of us in the committee I believe had in mind, that it should be considered as being directly attributable to the airport.
I want to raise only one other point which I raised before. I would have hoped that the minister would give what weight he considers advisable at least to suggestions that are made with the design of making the legislation better than it is.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ZONING OF AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with the previous speakers in objecting to the wording of this paragraph. I am quite sure the minister realizes the difficulty of drafting a paragraph that will satisfy the officials in the department and at the same time satisfy the members of the opposition. I think anyone reading this at first will certainly be puzzled when he comes to the word "minus". The phrase there is, "minus an amount equal to any increase in the value of the property". That would be minus an amount equal to any increase in value brought about by the creation of the airport.
It seems to me that there is no relation to the two things. We have airports now in existence and in the future we are going to have zoning regulations. As a result of those zoning regulations the theory is that damage may be done to property. If there were 55704-176i
Aeronautics Act
damage to property the owner would be entitled to compensation as a result of the zoning regulation.
But then the government says, "We are not finished, we must go back and see what if anything you got when the airport was constructed perhaps ten, fifteen or twenty years ago". It seems to me that that is mixing two things which should not be mixed up. For example, you might have two persons owning property, both being equally affected by the regulation. One man may have owned his property before the airport was built while the other man might be a recent purchaser. The first man would get compensation equal to the damage which his property had suffered as a result of the zoning regulation. But the other man would be asked when he had bought his property, and when he replied that he bought it since the airport had been built he would be told that his case was different, that he must take off part of the compensation he would get.

These restrictions are akin to the restrictions imposed by municipalities, and that is why I make the statement that this is a new field. I think we are entitled at least to a trial in order to see how it will work out.
Hon. members say that this is unfair because it gives with the one hand and takes away with the other. It does not provide any such thing, if you read the bill carefully, and I say this with all respect to those who have spoken. It has been suggested by an hon. member that if a person suffers damage to his property to the extent of $1,000, that $1,000 might be wiped out if the "minus" provision was applied. That is not a proper interpretation to put on the paragraph.
I would think that the proper interpretation to put on it is this. The moment we decide to zone an airport and pass a regulation we register a plan and the regulations which will indicate how the airport will be affected by the zoning that has been described in committee and here, that is, the horizontal zone limiting buildings to one hundred and fifty feet; the zone at the end of the flightway where buildings may go up one foot for every 50 feet out; and the zone on the side of the flightway where they can go up a foot for every 7 feet 'out.
Let me take the case quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. Supposing these zoning regulations affect 30 acres of a farm of 100 acres; roughly speaking, a little less than one-third of the farm is
affected and the "minus" would apply only to that one-third and not to the two-thirds as suggested by my hon. friend. In other words, what the regulation will apply to is the plan with the description which will be deposited in the registry office, which in that particular case would be the one-third. The "minus" will apply to the same portion of the land as will the "plus". For that reason I think the section is properly worded.
It has been suggested that there will be discrimination between owners of adjacent properties, the one who may have bought his farm a long time ago and the one who may have bought it recently. I do not see that any distinction is being made at all. If an original owner disposed of his land one or two months ago he benefited by the increase in the value of the farm just as an original owner will benefit proportionately in the increased value of the farm if affected by these regulations. I cannot see any distinction between adjacent owners, one who bought the day before yesterday and the other who has held his property for years. The one who bought the day before yesterday paid the increased value attributable to the airport. Therefore the original owner will lose absolutely nothing, and so far as the new purchaser is concerned, why should he gain by it? He has just purchased the land at the time the regulations are put into effect so there is no discrimination against him.

I indicated in the committee that I had no objection to adding the word "directly", but counsel for the Department of Transport indicated that the word would make no difference because the court would have to take cognizance of what was attributable. The committee decided against that amendment, and in the face of their decision I cannot come forward and suggest that the word "directly" should be inserted now. I do not think I should do that.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 289, to amend the Canada-France Income Tax Convention Act, 1951.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to approve the codicil to the income tax convention between Canada and France. The convention was approved by parliament as chapter 40 of the statutes of 1951, assented to June 30, 1951. Under the convention a French enterprise will only be taxed in Canada with respect to its industrial, mining, commercial or financial profits to the extent that these are attributable to its permanent establishment in Canada. Similarly, a Canadian enterprise will only be taxed in France with respect to similar profits attributable to its permanent establishment in France.
Now, I should like to point out to the house that the change in this bill has to do entirely with what constitutes a permanent establishment, either in France or in Canada. The term "permanent establishment" was defined in paragraph VI of article 2 of the original agreement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CANADA-FRANCE INCOME TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1951
speechtext: Is that the agreement attached to the act?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CANADA-FRANCE INCOME TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1951
speechtext:
That is the agreement we passed a year ago, and it is attached to the act.
The codicil to the convention, which is the subject of the present bill, adds a further refinement to this definition of "permanent establishment". It provides-this is the change-that a Canadian enterprise shall not be deemed to have a permanent establishment in France, if the contract for the sale of goods is settled in Canada, even though the goods are kept in storage in France for the convenience of delivery and not for publicity purposes. The same rule applies to a French enterprise selling in Canada. A company may have an agent in the other country to solicit orders which are transmitted to the home country for final acceptance. A similar provision was included in the income tax agreement between Canada and New Zealand, and it is also found in the agreement made between Great Britain and France.
Canada-France Tax Agreement
The convention is not yet in force. It will come into force upon an exchange of notes between the Canadian and French governments, which exchange will take place when the necessary legislation has been passed in both countries. I might also add that, as to the action being taken by the French government to bring the convention into force, we have been advised by the Department of External Affairs that Mr. Pinay, the French Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, stated in the French national assembly on May 9, 1952, approximately as follows, and I quote:
The convention signed between France and Canada on the 14th March, 1951, could not be submitted for the approval of the French parliament because it was thought desirable, in advance, to complete and clarify certain of its provisions. However, agreement on the matters in doubt can now be considered as having been definitely settled and everything will be done to complete the necessary proceedings for putting the convention into force within as short a delay as possible.

As the resolution says, this is a prelude to the amendment and codification of the present Immigration Act. It relates only in part to immigration policy. To a very large extent it relates to the administration of immigration. It has certain provisions of a financial character, such as those mentioned in the resolution. But these are not departures in principle; they are merely an insertion in the act of authority for expenditures which are now made by the estimates and do not reflect a change in policy.
There are certain provisions in the bill which would facilitate the handling of cases in Canada, so that we will not have as much delay in the transactions with persons who are either ordered deported or allowed to land. The information we have on the subject would seem to reveal that there were far more civilians than there were personnel of the department involved in these irregularities. The answer to that question was as follows:
It is not considered to be in the public interest to disclose such information.
If the reason for that answer is that the investigation into the way in which these persons were involved, and any legal consequences which should follow, was not complete, and that for that reason it was not in the public interest to disclose the information, the answer would be acceptable. But if it is intended by that answer that it is not generally considered in the public interest that that type of information should be disclosed, then I for one do not accept that answer. The fact is that some 75 persons were admitted illegally to Canada. They may have been legally qualified to enter this country, but nevertheless they were admitted illegally because of irregularities engaged in by a small number of persons in the employ of the department. In proportion to the seriousness of the crime, there was a comparatively large number of civilians, both in this country and in Europe, who were involved.

There is another administrative matter which is bothering the people of Canada. I refer to the lack of administrative machinery to ensure that immigrants that have been brought to this country on the understanding that they will work in a particular job for a certain length of time remain in that employment during that time. I am thinking particularly of farm labour. There seems to be a fairly widespread trend among immigrants who have been brought here to work on farms for a certain period to drift into the cities before that period has elapsed.
Another matter to be considered is the inadequate provision for the assistance of immigrants coming to this country to work as domestic help. I know of instances where couples have come out to work in Canadian households. Their work has been found most satisfactory and the arrangement was continuing quite well. I have been impressed with the way in which Canadian householders have given every assistance to immigrants to learn English' and to qualify themselves as rapidly as possible as good citizens.
Perhaps I may be forgiven for mentioning this other matter, but apparently, owing to the good food and perhaps the climate, it has happened in the case of many couples that pregnancies have occurred in Canada without similar pregnancies having occurred for many years previously in Europe. There have been many of these blessed events. However, they present a tremendous problem to householders in Canada who are employing these people. In cases which have come to my attention the medical advice has been that the woman immigrant should no longer continue to work. What is the householder to do? He cannot turn these people out on the street, and yet he is sometimes unable to arrange alternative accommodation.
I know of cases where householders have asked welfare agencies what can be done and have applied also to the department. I understand that there is only one person in the department to look after the welfare of all displaced persons in the immediate district. That person is simply snowed under. There is no suggestion that she is not making every effort to assist these people; the fact is that she simply cannot cope with the situation. Eventually one case I know of was dealt with by a private welfare agency in the city. It seems to me that some provision should be made by the department for the assistance of immigrants coming to this country and finding themselves in difficult circumstances so that the position of both the immigrant and the Canadian householder will be relieved.
It is indicated that the legislation contemplates a system of assisted passage and

This matter comes directly within the provisions of the resolution, which states that the legislation is to provide for the making of loans to immigrants in respect of the costs of their transportation. A circular letter-it was not even an original letter- was sent to this employer stating that he was expected to undertake and agree to make certain deductions from the pay of the immigrant employee and turn that over to the department monthly. In addition he was to undertake and agree to provide the department with certain specific information with respect to the immigrant.
I think Canadians have shown a commendable willingness to take on and train displaced persons and assist them in becoming useful and valuable citizens of Canada. A circular letter making the demand that they undertake and agree to do certain things is not calculated to further that policy and that attitude on the part of Canadian employers.
I wish to point out that in this case it was not the employer who had put in a request for this immigrant as an employee. The immigrant came to this employer who had certain vacancies in his establishment and asked if he could be given a job. He was given a job and a short time later this circular letter came along making these demands. I do not think the department should be making these demands of Canadian employers who are trying to help out immigrants in this way.
The contact should be between the department and the immigrant. It could be suggested to the immigrant that he approach the employer and ask him if he is willing to make these deductions and turn them over to the department for the immigrant. If that were done there could be no objection, but I agree with the gentleman who drew this matter to my attention that it is quite uncalled for that these sudden demands be made by a mimeographed circular letter when he has given a job to a newly-arrived immigrant.

To answer briefly some of the questions that have been raised, and to deal first with the question just asked by the hon. member for Eglinton, it is desirable to admit immigrants at the time when the period of waiting between their arrival and employment will be the minimum. It has always been the policy to concentrate, if possible, the admission of immigrants from roughly the first of February until some time in the late summer. That was not possible last year for a number of reasons including the fact that those who had been processed early in the year did not have transportation facilities and when the fall came they insisted on using their visas and coming forward even in the face of the knowledge that perhaps during the winter months it would be difficult to place them.
There was one other factor. The shipping that was under the control of the IRO became available in the fall for a much larger number of persons and, as I have said, they elected to come forward, unexpectedly to some extent, in the fall months rather than in the winter and spring. My hon. friend referred to the month of April, but may I suggest to him that farm workers particularly can be placed throughout the winter. The farming communities want to have men at the very earliest beginning of the spring work, and farmers are willing to take them in the winter months, even if they do not get what they consider full value for their money for a few weeks, in order to be sure that they have them when the season begins. We have had no difficulties whatever in placing farm workers throughout the year, and for that reason we have tried particularly this year to bring in farm workers in the early winter months and those who have other employment skills in the main in the later months. That is the policy, and it will be followed this year.

I want to ask the minister a question with regard to certain people, namely Latvians, Estonians, and Lithuanians. I had a case brought to my attention of a young Latvian man who came to this country and established himself in my own home town of Sussex, as a matter of fact. He is well established. He was promised that he could bring out his family, his father, his mother and his brothers. After investigation it was decided that these people could be brought to this country; but I believe on further investigation it was found that this young man's father, a Latvian, had served with what is called the Latvian legion against the Russians, and served with the German army.
The facts of the matter are that Latvia was overrun by Russia, as hon. members know,

in 1940. Later on the Germans came into the country and conscripted those Latvians. It was not voluntary service that was given, it was compulsory and it was against the Russians who had overrun their country. This young man's father, like many others, belonged to the so-called Latvian legion which was fighting against the Russians whom he considered his oppressors. He had never fought against any other people except Russia, but on account of fighting against an ally of ours at that time the people in this Latvian legion are prevented from coming to this country as immigrants; at least that is my understanding.
The United States immigration authorities take an entirely different view of that matter from the immigration authorities here in Canada. I hold in my hand a document which reads:
The true nature of the Latvian legion was also studied under scrutiny by the United States displaced persons commission. The latter has made in its decision of September 1, 1950, the following statement:
"Baltic Waffen-SS units (Baltic legion) are to be considered as separate and distinct in purpose, ideology, activities and qualification for membership from German SS, and therefore: The displaced persons commission holds them not to be a movement hostile to the government of the United States under section 13 of the displaced persons act of 1948, as amended."
The result is that these people are allowed to migrate to the United States, but so far they have not been allowed to migrate to this country. This is creating a hardship. I should like to ask the minister whether he has studied this situation, and whether any further study will be given it. I have a number of papers here which were given to me by this young man from my home town of Sussex, which say that his father is a man of very high education, and I believe he would make a desirable citizen.
There is another matter which they sort of take as proof against these people whom we would desire to have in this country. They say they were German sympathizers. There is the fact that some sort of blood test was made, and they have the German symbol on their arm which shows that they belong to a certain blood group, and so on. Whether or not the minister has any knowledge of this I do not know. If he has, I should like to have his comments. Frankly the case of this young man and his family, along with others who I believe have made application, might be reconsidered.

While I realize it is dangerous to particularize about one case, I have in mind an immigrant who came here, developed tuberculosis and was hospitalized. The minister will perhaps recall that the case was brought to his attention. This man had been getting along well in this country, but apparently he had a lesion which became active with the result that he was hospitalized in one of the sanatoria in Ontario on a temporary basis. That happens to be one case, but it seems to me unfair that when an immigrant has been given a clean bill of health by our immigration service overseas, and subsequently in this country develops tuberculosis, an order for deportation should be mandatory. In the case to which I have referred stay

of deportation was granted. When the textile people were here in the wintertime they complained about immigration, and also about the unemployment in that industry. speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ESTABLISH- MENT OP RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.
speechtext:
The proposed legislation arises out of the report of the MacQuarrie committee and is intended to give, in large measure, legislative form to the recommendations made in that report. You will remember, sir, that this committee was appointed in June of 1950 to study the Canadian combines legislation and recommend what amendments, if any, should be made in order to make it a more effective instrument for the encouraging and safeguarding of our free economy. The MacQuarrie committee made its final report last March, and that report was tabled during the present session.
The conclusions of the MacQuarrie committee may be fairly summarized briefly as follows:
1.	The committee affirmed the principles of the present legislation.
2.	It recommended that the two functions of investigation and report, which are at present joined in the commissioners, should be separated. This recommendation involves no diminution of the powers of the combines commission. It relates, rather, to internal organization.
3.	The report recommends certain additional measures for the strengthening of the combines legislation.
I am sure it is unnecessary for me at this stage to review the history of the MacQuarrie committee but, out of deference to the persons who composed it and to the, as I think, splendid work which they accomplished, I wish again at this time to mention their names. The chairman was Mr. Justice J. H. MacQuarrie of the supreme court of Nova Scotia, and the other members of the committee were Dr. W. A. Mackintosh, who is now principal of Queen's university; G. F. Curtis, dean of the faculty of law of the university of British Columbia, and Maurice Lamontagne, now director of the department of economics of Laval university.
Speaking generally, the proposals are directed toward an important internal reorganization of the present combines investigation commission and to strengthening the legislation and the commission in a number of important respects.
Although we have become accustomed to speaking about the combines investigation commission, there is in fact no such entity and the word "commission" is mentioned nowhere in our combines legislation. There is only one commissioner in whom all the

Combines Investigation Act powers conferred by the legislation are now centred. All the other officers who have functions under the act are completely subordinate to him and under his direction.
This system has obvious advantages and it has obvious disadvantages. The MacQuarrie committee came to the conclusion that, on the whole, the disadvantages outweigh the advantages. They expressed the opinion that the union of functions to which I refer is a basic weakness of the legislation, being neither right in principle nor sound administratively. Its effect, by imposing disparate duties upon the commissioner, is to place him in an equivocal position. In saying this I am paraphrasing certain parts of the report because I do not think the case can be put better than the MacQuarrie committee has put it.
In the first place, the commissioner determines the over-all policy that governs the operation of the commission. Having regard to the work which the commission can accomplish, he selects those parts of the economy and those industries that are to be the subject of investigation. This obviously is a function which calls for the exercise of initiative and drive. In other words, in respect of those functions the commissioner may not be passive; he must be active. He has a definite job to perform.
While recognizing the competence with which we have been served to date in the administration of the combines legislation, the MacQuarrie committee went on to point out that the person now responsible for making reports has been and must necessarily be closely involved in both the initiation and conduct of the investigation. However impartial he may be in reaching his conclusions, his prior association with the investigation work itself provides a basis for possible criticism. As the committee put it so succinctly, in the case of a single commissioner, he is given the compromising appearance of being "at one and the same time prosecutor and judge", and no matter how fully his assessment of a situation may be justified by results, its value is lessened by the inconsistency of his position. These reports which go out to the public have important and serious consequences for the persons with whom they deal. It is important, therefore, not only that the reports be fair, unbiased and impartial-and I am satisfied that they have always been that-but it is equally important that everyone who reads the reports be absolutely convinced that this is the case.
The way to make sure of this is to provide- as we now propose to do, following the MacQuarrie committee recommendations-that the

authors of the report will have no responsibility other than that of simply interpreting the facts.
Incidental to the foregoing, the committee goes on to remark that the separation of the two functions of investigation and appraisal would effect a logical, efficient and economical division of work. In this respect the commissioner informs me that, having regard to the number of matters now pending in the commission, the preparation of reports, in itself, adds up to the time of at least three persons corresponding to the three members of the board which the MacQuarrie committee is recommending.
The report of the MacQuarrie committee lays great stress on the important position which would be occupied by the board which has been recommended. The committee pointed to the great advantage which results from drawing on the knowledge and judgment of a group of competent persons in appraising the complex problems involved in restrictive trade practices. While the committee recommended that the board as a whole would prepare a report, it was also recommended that there be power of delegation with respect to hearings and other administrative proceedings so that the different members of the board could be engaged in different inquiries prior to the report stage. In this way the full value of the combined judgment of the board would be brought to bear with respect to appraisal and the framing of recommendations but, at the same time, the division of duties among members of the board will provide for more expeditious handling of the inquiries which may be in progress.
The need for undertaking research projects and other general studies bearing upon monopoly and combines problems afforded, in the opinion of the committee, an additional reason why there should be a division of the work.
So much for internal organization.
In addition to the matter of internal organization, it is proposed to strengthen the legislation and its administration in the following important respects.
1,	provision of a new remedy whereby, while an offence is in the incipent stage, the court can order it to be discontinued; and whereby the court, in addition to the penalty imposed in a prosecution, can order a situation which has been created in contravention of the act to be dissolved.
2,	provision to remove the present ceilings upon fines.
3,	provision to extend the powers of investigation to enable the administration to investigate not only offences that have been

committed, but also the development of situations which may be expected to give rise to offences in the future.
4,	provision to permit a court before whom any person is convicted of a combines offence to require such person to make continuing returns relating to his business.
5,	provision for amendment of section 498A of the Criminal Code. In this respect paragraph (a) of subsection 1 relating to discriminatory discounts now applies to a single transaction. This may have the effect of preventing a vendor from lowering his price to meet the price of a competitor even where such a step is necessary in order to retain the business involved. As amended, the paragraph will be directed against the practice of discrimination. This, I would submit, is what the section was really aimed at in the beginning and it is hoped that with this change the section, which has seen little use, will be more practical and will serve the original intention behind it.
In this statement I have not exhausted the changes which the proposed legislation will make, but I have, I think, gone as fully into them as I should do at this stage.

subtopic: ESTABLISH- MENT OP RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments on the statement by the minister will be brief. I do not think the statement he has made calls for extensive discussion in the house, and I know that many hon. members desire to put questions to the minister in committee. I shall therefore content myself with several brief observations and no more.
The minister has paid some tribute to the MacQuarrie committee. I am sure that all hon. members recognize the importance of the service which has been rendered by the members of this committee, and appreciate the sense of public duty and public service which animated the authors of the report.
Last autumn, in the course of discussion in this house on an interim report of this committee, I had occasion to make some comment upon the work of the committee and to express regret at that time that the committee had committed itself to a particular remedy, not having yet surveyed the entire field referred to it. I also suggested in one of the committees of the houses, which was studying the same subject, that I thought the MacQuarrie committee could have been strengthened had there been someone on that committee who had experience in direct merchandising. The practical experience of such a person I think would have been of very great value and assistance to the committee in seeking to arrive at comprehensive recommendations in the light of problems that have arisen in the course of administration of
Combines Investigation Act this important legislation. But while I retain the opinion I then expressed, Mr. Speaker, I naturally join with the minister and others in expressing tribute to the sense of public duty which has animated the authors of this report.
In the second place, sir, as the minister has indicated, we are largely concerned in the present discussion with means of improving the machinery for investigating combines or incipient combines in this country. There can be no question, Mr. Speaker, that we must always be on the alert for means of improving the machinery provided by legislation for this purpose. I do not care how suitable the machinery may be on paper, the drive behind the legislation is always going to be more important than mere questions of machinery. Nevertheless, sir, in its report the MacQuarrie committee has put its finger on a place where the present machinery does naturally give rise to some question as to whether it is the most efficient that can be devised for the purpose.
The problem of the union of diverse functions in the present commissioner is one that I am sure has added not a little to the complexity of the duties of the commissioner, and has probably led to not a little difficulty or delay in carrying out the terms of the legislation. It is important, as the minister has said, that the commissioner should not be put in an equivocal position, and it seems to me that in its report the committee has placed its finger on a situation where at least superficially the case they have made out for a change is strong.
The minister has also very properly said that on the reporting side of the functions of the present commissioner it is so important that the reports should be fair and impartial. I do not withdraw anything that I have said on any previous occasion about the importance of publicity; and I trust that, in keeping with the recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee, this new legislation will not subtract one whit from the requirements of the present legislation in regard to publication of reports. The minister nods, indicating that the legislation will not tamper with that important provision of the present legislation. But the requirements of the act, in reference to the publication of reports, do serve to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, the vital importance of fairness and impartiality in these reports, and the division of functions that is now proposed into the investigation and research agency on the one hand and the board on the other will serve, I think, to relieve the present situation where, as has been said, the commissioner might find himself in a sense in the position of being both prosecutor and judge.

Combines Investigation Act
I am not going to make any extended comment upon the observations made by the minister in regard to changes of substance in the present law. There will be a better opportunity, I take it, to review those changes when the bill has been placed before hon. members.
There is one feature that may perhaps be deserving of comment, Mr. Speaker. It is the recommendation at page 63 of the report that research should be carried on in the field of monopolistic situations. I find there, under the heading "General recommendations" this interesting recommendation:
1. That research in the field of monopolistic situations and practices should become one of the most important assignments of the investigation and research agency.
Without spending too long on that recommendation, it does occur to me that the division of functions now proposed will make possible a work of research which has not, I fancy, been possible hitherto.
Finally I think what has happened since last December with respect to a particular aspect of the field covered by this legislation is not unworthy of comment. Last December there were proposals and pleas on the part of the official opposition that the amendments then offered to the house should not be hurried into enactment. We urged that time should be given for adequate consideration and review. Nevertheless the government was adamant, and insisted that those amendments should be enacted into law before the prorogation of the session. It will be recalled that we were here engaged on that task until December 29. We urged at that time that the situation sought to be dealt with by the legislation was not so urgent that it could not await more study and consideration. And now we find that after those amendments have been in effect for five months, there has not been one prosecution. There is only one inquiry afoot, and there has been nothing to report as to what has been done under that legislation.
It seems to me this completely explodes that sense of great urgency which the government sought to create last December, and which had the effect at that time of denying that legislation the adequate consideration a matter of that importance should have warranted, particularly when it involved the denial of a hearing to many important organizations who had what they considered to be representations of value to place before the committee of the house charged with the responsibility of reviewing the proposed legislation, and the alleged need of it.
I trust that in approaching this question and the whole field now covered by the final

report of the MacQuarrie committee there will be adequate opportunity of weighing all the proposals, and that we will not be rushed into enacting legislation, as we were on that occasion, without proper and adequate consideration.
There is one purpose which we of the official opposition will have directly in view in studying the legislation which is to follow the introduction of this resolution; that is that none of the safeguards provided by the present legislation in respect of access to the courts should be denied. We will scrutinize this legislation carefully, to make sure that nothing by way of right of access to the courts is denied to anyone who may be said to be within the scope of the legislation.

subtopic: ESTABLISH- MENT OP RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of years we in the C.C.F. have been asking for more effective legislation to prevent combines, cartels and monopolies in restraint of trade. I have not seen the legislation the minister proposes to introduce into the house, but from what he has told us I should think it would be an improvement on what we have had in the past. That is all to the good; we welcome legislation which will make action against combines more effective. We welcome legislation which will make penalties against combines more effective because, to say the least, in the past some of the penalties have been footling in their nature. What I would like to see is combines legislation with teeth in it; not false teeth, or teeth which can be disposed of. But pending the time the legislation comes down, I shall not say anything about that.
I would like to bring to the minister's attention the case of an industry about which I reminded him last October. When we reach the committee stage I should like to learn from him how the new legislation will affect a situation such as I shall describe. I am going to place on record tonight figures which I maintain make a prima facie case that there is a combine in the electrical industry.
How it can be proved in terms of the law, I do not know. But if the law cannot use my figures to punish those who I believe are breaking it, then to my mind the law is an ass. The figures I shall use were tabled in the Manitoba legislature on March 20 of this year on motion of Mr. Swailes. Mr. Speaker, there are just a couple of comments which I think should be made in addition to those made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). Before embarking upon my general remarks, one thing took place today about which I should like to make some observation and also suggest to the minister that he has somewhat overlooked the proper rights and interests of members of parliament in connection with this important subject, and I am referring to members on the government side as well as on this side of the house.
This afternoon the minister tabled two copies of the report on the investigation into an alleged combine in the manufacture, distribution and sale of rubber products. When questioned as to whether this would be available for distribution to hon. members, the minister said that it was a bulky document-it certainly is, running to 710 pages-and that copies had been duplicated and made available to all members of the press gallery. But I point out that there are no copies available for all the members of this house.
I think it is proper to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that members of this house should not be overlooked when reports of this kind are tabled in compliance with the terms of a statute and dealing with matters in which hon. members have great 
interest. We find that although at least 50 copies were mimeographed so as to be available to members of the press gallery, no steps were taken to run off a sufficient number to make them available to members of the house. If the minister does not feel that members of the house are more interested and more entitled to these copies than members of the press gallery, perhaps he will feel that we should run at least next in priority and that when he was making 50 copies he might have run off an extra 250 or 260 copies so that members of the house would have it available, particularly when a discussion of this very matter was to take place by way of a resolution and bill to be introduced into the House of Commons.
In making a few general observations on the subject matter of the resolution I wish first to support what has been said by the hon. member for Eglinton as to the general position of this party with respect to the subject. I wish to make some general observations without at the present time going into any details. I think it essential in considering legislation dealing with combines, monopolies and restrictive trade practices that specific attention should be devoted to the question of whether or not there should be a review of public policy. I do not retract or depart from previous expressions of mine and expressions of principle which have been made in this house as to the dangers-and they are real dangers-and potential evils of combines, monopolies and other such things.
There has been a conflict in policy for many years. It was the late President Theodore Roosevelt who initiated the antitrust legislation in the United States which dealt with the whole subject of the preservation of small businesses and the danger of trusts and combines getting control of the economy of the country. Nevertheless it was recognized even then, as was said at the time, that the mere fact of bigness is not of itself an offence. I think we must be careful in all our legislation to see to it that the position should never arise where a person or firm, which acts fairly, honestly and openly, which never artificially depresses wages or artificially increases prices, and which acts throughout in accordance with the public interest, might be guilty of a technical offence against our legislation. I think we have to be careful that we do not go that far in this country. I therefore suggest to the minister by way of observation that perhaps there should be more emphasis, either in the title of the legislation or in the title of the commission to be set up, on the question of fairness because it seems to me that what the

legislation should be directed against in the main is practices which are unfair to competitors, to the consumer and to the wage earner.
I for one should like to see somewhat more emphasis placed on the question of whether the practices complained of are, in the particular case, adverse to the public interest. Having said that, I think it is probably not appropriate at this time with Your Honour in the chair to make any detailed comments upon the recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee other than to say that, like the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), I am very glad indeed to see that the recommendations contain a specific clause recommending the preservation of the provision with regard to the publication of the reports. It seems to me that if the legislation follows out the recommendations of the committee and separates the functions of initial investigation from the functions of the board with respect to a general review of whether or not there has been an offence, then with the board reporting on that aspect of the matter some of the objection to immediate publication which has previously existed is now removed.
That being the case, I am thoroughly in accord with the recommendation that the time for publication of the board's reports be the same as in the present act. Like the hon. member for Eglinton, and perhaps because he and I took some considerable part in the discussion of the legislation last fall arising out of the interim report of the MacQuarrie committee dealing with the practice of resale price maintenance, I should also like to refer to one consideration in that regard. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that it was frequently and earnestly requested by the official opposition that there should be the fullest opportunity, both in the special committee which was set up and in the discussion in the house, for a full inquiry into this whole field before we rushed into legislation the enactment of which the government had recommended.
We were told there was no necessity for any such inquiry. In particular we said that before the legislation dealing with resale price maintenance was enacted there should be an opportunity for investigation into the danger, which might arise as a result of that legislation, of a resumption of the loss leader practice, and that at the same time as the legislation dealing with resale price maintenance, legislation should be introduced to safeguard merchants, particularly the independent retailer, against the evils of loss leadering. You will recall, sir, that after various threats of closure and various comments that sufficient time had
Combines Investigation Act been taken, although up to that point there had only been two and a half days of discussion in the house, after both our friends to the left as well as the government had sought devices to curtail discussion in the house, the legislation did become law just after Christmas. It is interesting in that regard to find that the MacQuarrie committee, upon whose interim report that legislation was based, now makes a recommendation on this matter to be found on page 64 of their report which has been tabled in the house. It is recommendation No. 3 under the heading "general", and reads as follows:
That the "loss leader" practice should be referred by the minister for thorough study by the proposed agency and board with a view to determining its prevalence and its effects and to recommending to the minister suitable amendment, if necessary, of the act.
That is exactly what we asked to be done last fall. This recommendation of the MacQuarrie committee fully justifies the stand we took last December in the house and at the hearings of the special committee appointed to consider the interim report. That is particularly so when you bear in mind the fact that, as the minister told the house a few days ago, there has been only one investigation and no prosecutions as a result of the legislation passed last fall to which at the time, according to the government propaganda, such importance was attached, and which was designed to curtail so many and such vicious practices.
When you realize that its results have been practically nil, and then find that the MacQuarrie committee now says a study should be made of the loss leader practice, then I think it becomes perfectly clear that the artificial haste with which last fall's legislation was passed was entirely uncalled for, and that the representations of the official opposition with respect to the interests and the position of the independent retailer, and the dangers from which he might suffer as a result of the loss leader practice, were well founded. I hope that opportunities to consider this legislation, important as I recognize it to be, will not be curtailed in the same manner as were opportunities for the consideration of the legislation last fall.
Before Your Honour leaves the chair I would ask the minister to say whether it is intended to refer this legislation to a special committee or one of the standing committees of the house. I should imagine there is probably no standing committee in existence under our rules which is designed to cope with such legislation, and that therefore it might be desirable to refer it to a special committee. I do not imagine this subject will be as controversial as the one last fall,

Combines Investigation Act and I would therefore hope that the study by the committee might be more valuable and, shall I say, more impartial. I feel that considerable advantage to the government, the house and the country might follow from a not time-consuming but thorough study of this legislation by a committee set up for the purpose. I would appreciate it if the minister would say a word on that subject before Your Honour leaves the chair.

375. Branch administration, $23,545.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At the last sitting of the committee of supply we had a discussion on this item. We had a discussion on national parks. There are still a few items connected with national parks; they go from 375 to 380. The first is a vote of $23,545 for branch administration.

I do not wish to delay the passage of this item, but there are one or two comments I should like to make about the national parks, particularly the mountain national park in the Rockies. We have in the Rockies some of the finest terrain in the world, not only for climbing in the summer
[The Chairman..]

but for skiing or ski-mountaineering in the winter. The one defect or problem in regard to the parks at the moment is their inaccessibility.
There has been a general theory that the parks should be maintained in their natural state, a theory to which no one can take serious exception. Yet it is very little good having a vast territory maintained in its natural state if it is inaccessible. The vastnesses of Tibet and the mountains behind the Karakoram may be very beautiful and may have wonderful scenic possibilities; but if they are inaccessible they are of little use to mankind.
The same applies to our national parks. The criticism has been made that if we render the national parks more accessible-that is, those of the national parks more than five hundred yards from a motor highway or a line of railway-the natural beauty of those parks will have been destroyed. To this I take grave objection. I believe that today we are passing from the economy of the horse to the economy of the motor vehicle. Obviously we cannot build roads into national parks through mountains without extremely heavy expense. But if those roads were built we would possibly open up the parks only on a comparatively limited scale. There are a number of places where roads must be built. The valley of the Ten Peaks is an example where a beautiful road has been built. Then there is the Banff-Jasper highway, the road into Little Yoho, the road up to the Emerald lakes, as well as many others which do open up beautiful terrain for the benefit of the tourist.
But they open up only a postage-stamp sized area of the great national heritage which is ours. Today, with the tremendous costs of a pack train, and the great expense of equipping a horse transport into areas of our national parks-and I am referring to Yoho and Jasper parks on both sides of the continental divide, as well as Banff national park -except to a few fortunate persons who may be members of organizations such as the Alpine club, we are precluding the vast proportion of our people from seeing the parks at all.
I suggest to the minister that today the best access to the parks is by air. If small airstrips could be built at different places in our great wilderness, it would be advantageous in the matter of viewing our parks. The Canadian Pacific Railway likes to advertise them as fifty Switzerlands in one. Well, they may be fifty Switzerlands, but fifty Switzerlands will do one no good unless he can see them. And they will do Canadians no good, or our visitors from elsewhere in the world, unless they can be seen.

Therefore I should like to see some method by which the most remote parts of the parks may be visited by people of moderate means. The only way those people may reach the remote places is by air. It may sound strange, but to equip the very smallest pack train for two people today would cost in the neighbourhood of $100 a day, and to go any considerable distance it would cost a great deal more than that. Without the assistance of a guide-and they are very scarce-there is the impossibility of travelling far from the beaten track.
If we are to develop our great heritage I suggest the department should encourage the construction of airstrips in the national parks, so that people of moderate means could reach them and see what there is to see. The criticism has been made that this would open the parks to undesirable types of travellers, and that it might deplete the lakes which at present are teeming with some of the finest game fish in the world. Attention has been called to the fire hazard, and there has been the objection that to facilitate air travel in the parks might damage the wildlife.
If these airstrips are made available, then at the same time they are made available to game wardens and park wardens to an even greater extent than to any person who might have predatory instincts. The policing of the parks would be much simpler than at the present time, when the wardens have to trek in many miles and for many hours to see whether someone has hurt himself or has brought in illicit weapons to hunt in the park. With airstrips placed throughout the parks firefighting would be made much easier. Any careless individual can start a fire, but it takes an organization to put it out. With airstrips we would be able to get over the mountains and your machinery for fighting fire would be greatly enhanced.
I suggest that the government seriously consider the construction of airstrips throughout the parks as a means of developing this great heritage. It would be infinitely cheaper than highway construction and would provide easier access than would be possible by foot or on horseback. If the record of flying in the Rocky mountains up to date is any criterion, it would be much safer.
I really love these national parks and I have travelled more than 2,000 miles through them by ski and on foot. We have a heritage which is unique in all the world. It is infinitely superior, it is wilder and more rugged than the parks in the United States, although their individual mountains may be higher. We should take steps to see that these parks are made available to people

Supply-Resources and Development of moderate means. We have these wildernesses but they do not do anyone any good.
The tourist comes to the big hotel to play golf, to look at a fashion show or to attend a convention. Many of them are willing to pay $20 a day to stop at one of these large hotels run by the railroads. But such a person knows nothing of the real beauty of our national parks, and he will not until facilities are made available for him to learn something about them. We are still operating these parks more or less as closed areas.
To me commercialism is anathema. I hate to see commercial signposts, and would be willing to do anything to prevent any type of commercialism because I know many objectionable things have happened already; but this heritage should be made available to Canadians and to visitors at reasonable rates. I suggest that the construction of airstrips provides the easiest and best way of making our national parks more completely available.

Mr. Chairman, I want to come back to what I was saying on Thursday evening when you advised me to wait until this item was before the committee. I was referring to the damage done in our national parks by wild animals. The farmers in these different districts have suffered tremendous damage from deer and elk. The provincial governments say they have nothing to do with it, and I am afraid the dominion government will say the same thing. The farmers are left holding the bag.
If there is going to be a conference in the near future between the dominion and provincial governments I think this is something worth while to discuss, to see what can be done. If the dominion or provincial governments cannot feed these elk and deer I do not think they should expect the poor farmer to feed them. The number of animals in the reserve should be cut down.
I do not want to repeat what I said on Thursday night when I was advised to wait for this item. I have a petition here signed by 55 people who have had their crops ruined. They were not even allowed to shoot these animals when they came near their crops. This has been an exceptionally bad year in my province because half the crop was not threshed until this spring. These poor fellows had no crop at all to thresh. I should like to quote from an article in the Winnipeg Tribune as follows:
Settlers in outlying areas of Swan river valley should receive some compensation for the loss that resulted from deer and elk eating and trampling crops. The attitude of the provincial government in evading all responsibility in this connection is neither impressive nor fair.

Supply-Resources and Development
The fact is that the crops of many settlers were totally destroyed. The majority of these new farmers were dependent on the spring harvest to pay their winter's bills and finance this year's program.
The case for the settlers is a convincing one. Deer are the property of the province, and under provincial law the farmer cannot shoot the animals to protect his crop. He had to sit idly by this winter and see the fruits of a year's work being destroyed by game.
I do not want to labour the point, but I think a solution could be found if the matter were taken up by the dominion and provincial representatives when they next meet. An effort should be made to control these marauding deer and elk in Manitoba.

Mr. Chairman, I have a great deal of sympathy with the hon. member for Selkirk, but out on the prairies we have a different problem. They have an organization known as Ducks Unlimited. This may be a fine thing for the man with a shotgun but it is not so good for the farmer who is trying to raise crops. I have seen hundreds of acres of crops destroyed in a few days when thousands of ducks have come in.
I do not think there is a finer playground in the world than our national parks in Alberta, whether it be Jasper, Waterton Lakes or some of the others. I have spent a good deal of time fishing in the rivers and lakes of the national parks. I have always found good fishing around Jasper and Water-ton Lakes, but apparently the fishing around Banff is exceptionally poor. I have heard some caustic remarks made by United States people about the fishing in the vicinity of Banff. I realize that this applies to the lakes and rivers that can be reached by motorcar and that if you travel far enough from the highway you will find good fishing. Is the same work in restocking the lakes and rivers being done around Banff as apparently is being done at Jasper and Waterton Lakes?
The quick answer to that is yes.

I want to ask the minister a few questions with reference to Fundy national park in New Brunswick. I agree with the statement of the hon. member for York West regarding what a splendid boon our parks are. We are very proud of Fundy national park. The scenery there compares more than favourably with any park in Canada. The great difficulty is to get to the park. The roads leading to the national park are very poor with the result that very few people, particularly tourists, are taking advantage of it. This is a new park, the last one to be opened in Canada. That may be one reason for the condition of the roads; but it has now been open for two or three


years and I know that United States tourists who hope to go to Fundy national park drive a few miles over a dusty road and then turn back.
I should like to ask the minister if the federal government is doing anything to urge the provincial government to improve the roads. I know it is not the responsibility of the federal government to build roads outside the park; and I commend the minister for the building of some splendid roads in the park. As soon as one strikes the park limits one has very good wheeling. I should like to ask the minister whether there is any agreement with the provincial government for the construction of roads. If there is not, I would ask the federal government to take up that matter with the provincial government to see if something cannot be done. The hon. member for York West spoke about airstrips in national parks. That will be the only way to get into ours if something is not done about the roads.
I should also like to refer to the matter of conservation. I am rather surprised that two hon. members should suggest that there is too much wildlife in the national parks. We are very pleased that the wildlife is increasing in Fundy park in New Brunswick. As a matter of fact it is one of the finest moose areas in our province. We are hoping the moose will increase. For some years we have had a game law in New Brunswick prohibiting the killing of moose, but there is a parasite that is perhaps killing more moose than are killed by hunters. It has occurred to me that possibly the government might experiment in this national park in some way to see if they cannot preserve the moose. I fear the day may come in our province as well as in other provinces when the moose will be much like the caribou. They will be a thing of the past. I should like to have the minister's comment on these matters. First of all I should like to know whether any effort is being made to urge the provincial government to provide better roads leading to our national park in New Brunswick, and I should also like the minister to deal with the conservation of wildlife in national parks.

Perhaps I should deal first with the matter of Fundy park, and then answer some of the other questions raised. I was very pleased to hear the hon. member's remarks about Fundy national park. I take quite a personal interest in it, having had the privilege of participating in the opening. I also had the pleasure of visiting it last year, at which time I drove in from the west and left it toward the east. I found the roads in both directions to be quite good. As my hon. friend has said, the road in the park is

now paved and it is a first class road. There have been some informal discussions with officials of the provincial government about the roads leading to the park, but as my hon. friend intimated there is no way we can bring pressure upon them or tell them what to do with respect to their highways. However, I am sure they realize the value of the asset to them and have in mind the importance of providing good opportunities to enter the park.
With respect to the problem in Riding Mountain national park, once the animals get outside the limits of the park they are free game and come under the laws and regulations of provincial governments. Our wildlife officers have been keeping in close touch with the situation in Riding Mountain national park. There have been discussions with the officials of the Manitoba government about the subject, and in fact there will be discussions again this year. Permits- can be obtained from the provincial government to shoot animals, and I am sure the provincial government officials will be most co-operative in that respect. Surveys were carried out in the park in March, 1952 by our chief mam-malogist, and it was indicated then that the population of elk was about 4,560, a decrease of some 3-6 per cent from the estimated population for 1951. The provincial game administration reported that 1,355 elk were killed outside the park during last year's season by hunters whose licences have been returned. Only 70 per cent of the licences have been returned so far so the probable total killed would be about 2,000 elk to date.
