When this matter was last discussed in the house I asked certain questions about the peace garden grant, and also about the increased rates for tourist campers. I wonder if the minister is going to comment on those.

I shall be very glad to do that, Mr. Chairman. With respect to the peace garden, I must say that I believe it typifies, as well as anything with which I have had to do, the fact that economies make a good topic for popular discussion but when they are reduced to a particular item they are very unpopular indeed. Perhaps I should tell hon. members something of the background of the international peace garden, and then leave it to them and to the people of Canada generally to judge whether or not they would wish to contribute an additional $15,000 to this project this year in the light of the level of taxation prevailing to meet the demands and requirements upon the government.
The establishment of the international peace garden at Turtle Mountain was largely

Supply-Resources and Development the outcome of a convention of the national association of gardeners held at Toronto in the summer of 1929. Delegates from all parts of Canada to that convention agreed that it would be an excellent idea to have an international peace garden astride the Canadian-United States border, as near to the centre of the North American continent as possible, this undertaking to symbolize the friendship, long and unbroken, existing between Canada and the United States; and that such a development on the boundary would be a meeting place of legionnaires of both countries and various international societies.
Following various organizational meetings held in both countries a potential garden area of 2,340 acres was established in 1932, 888 acres in the state of North Dakota and 1,452 acres in Manitoba. This latter area was donated by the Manitoba government, being formerly part of the Turtle Mountain forest reserve. The formal dedication ceremony took place on July 14, 1942, before a group of 50,000 people who bore witness to the solemn pledge of two nations who would continue forever the peace which has existed between them for more than a century. A cairn about eight feet high, built of native stone gathered from both sides of the boundary and bearing a plaque with the inscription "To God and His glory we two nations dedicate this garden and pledge ourselves that as long as men shall live we shall not take up arms against one another" was unveiled on that occasion.
The original idea for financing this project put forward by the first board of directors was to raise approximately $5 million over a twenty-year period through weekly contributions by school children and adults scattered over the whole country, but the depression of the thirties resulted in this plan being abandoned.
The federal government, through the Department of Mines and Resources, has assisted financially in the development of the Canadian section of the peace garden by means of funds provided under the following votes: Vote 459, supplementary estimates 1936-37, $12,000; Vote 315, supplementary estimates 1937-38, $10,000; Vote 537, supplementary estimates 1938-39, $10,000; Vote 518, supplementary estimates 1939-40, $10,000; Vote 520, supplementary estimates 1939-40, $10,000. The additional vote for 1939-40 was to be devoted entirely to forestry conservation and reforestation under the provincial government. The grant was discontinued in 1940 and the reasons expressed by Mr. Crerar at the time were as follows:
That in view of the war, and the consequent heavy financial burden which this country is called
[Mr. Winters. J
upon to bear in connection with our preparedness, it was considered that the department would not be warranted in asking for further funds.
The grant was resumed in 1949 and continued to 1951-52 inclusive with the following amounts being provided: Vote 221, main estimates 1949-50, $15,000; Vote 369, main estimates 1950-51, $15,000; Vote 388, main estimates 1951-52, $15,000. That makes a total contribution to date on the part of the federal government to this project of $97,000. In addition the federal government has helped with materials, such as logs, nursery stock and of course advice from our officials in the national parks branch.
After an item for $15,000 had been included in the estimates for 1951-52 for the international peace graden, I wrote the president of the peace garden and informed him that I was extremely doubtful as to what further contributions he could expect in future years. This letter was written bearing in mind the international situation. When the estimates for 1952-53 were under consideration I could not recommend the inclusion of funds for the international peace garden in view of Canada's heavy commitments for defence and the resulting necessity for the federal government to curtail expenditures.
Moreover, the federal government is presently responsible for the operation of a very beautiful national park in Manitoba, the Riding Mountain national park, covering an area of 1,148 square miles. Over the years this park has required the expenditure of considerable public funds, and I presume it will continue to do so. For example, last year a total of $504,538 was spent on maintenance, operation, and construction; this year a further amount of $825,251 is being requested for these purposes.
There are also two national historic sites and parks maintained by the taxpayers of Canada. They are Fort Prince of Wales historic park at Churchill and Lower Fort Garry historic site, outside Winnipeg. When one considers these investments in national parks and, in addition, the $97,000 the federal government has already contributed toward the international peace garden, I am sure the taxpayers of Canada will conclude that the province of Manitoba is not being overlooked in this respect.

Just a minute. Are we to have nothing at all said on this item? It seems to me it is a most important matter. Can the minister not indicate just briefly what is being done, without necessarily reading a full report?

The committee will recall that this is a study of the conditions surrounding the flooding of greater Winnipeg and studies undertaken to determine what, if any, measures can be taken to reduce the hazard of flooding there in the future.
Are they joint studies with the United States authorities?

We have had a number of consultations with the United States authorities and there is the closest liaison there. I should be glad to give an up-to-date progress report, if that is what hon. members of the committee wish.
The first part of it deals with the main stem and eastern tributaries of the Red river.
Hydrographic survey of the Red river from lake Winnipeg to the international boundary, a distance of 155 miles, has been completed. Cross-sections were taken at 200-foot intervals through the city and suburbs, at 800 to 1000-foot intervals north of the city and at 1,000-foot intervals south of the city. All cross-sections have been plotted and standard hydrographic plans have been prepared showing river bed and bank contours with profiles of river bed, normal water level, 1950 flood level and general prairie level. Similar plans have been prepared of the Assiniboine river from its mouth to St. James compiled from hydrographic survey carried out by the greater Winnipeg diking board. From St. James to Headingley, the Assiniboine river has been cross-sectioned and the results have been plotted.
Surveys have been carried out east of Winnipeg over possible diversion routes. These surveys covered various possible intake


and outlet locations and provided for location of routes both east and west of the town of Transcona.
Levels have been taken throughout the city of St. Boniface and the Winnipeg suburbs, and with the information available for the city of Winnipeg, a contour map of the greater Winnipeg area has been prepared.
A topographic survey of the valley extending beyond the 1950 flood elevations has been completed and plans of this survey drawn.
A reconnaissance of subsoil conditions has been made over the possible diversion routes east of Winnipeg by wash bore drill and electrical resistivity apparatus. Several core holes were drilled by rotary diamond drill at locations indicated by wash bore where rock might be encountered.
A rotary core diamond drill was employed along the river between the Bergen cut-off and Lockport covering that area commonly referred to as Lister's rapids. From the results obtained the bedrock profile along the river bottom has been plotted.
A reconnaissance survey and a subsurface exploration by wash bore drill has been carried out over a possible diversion route from the Assiniboine river towards lake Winnipeg through the west end of the city.
A topographical survey is in progress for the eastern tributaries diversion. This diversion would tap the Roseau, the Rat, the Seine rivers and Joubert creek, and it would virtually control the greater percentage of the drainage basin on the east side of the Red river in Canada. It would divert the runoff from this area by means of dikes and a small canal to enter the Red river near lake Winnipeg by either Cook's creek or Devil's creek.
Miscellaneous field surveys are in progress to obtain data on all bridge crossings, subways and railroad grades within the greater Winnipeg area.
The staff of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration, which has been assisting this department in the Red river basin investigation, has continued its contribution in the surveys and studies of the Assiniboine and Pembina rivers.
A survey of the Assiniboine valley within Manitoba for the purpose of determining river flow characteristics, flood routing and valley storage capacities at high river stages has been completed.
Detailed topographic surveys with subsurface exploration by wash bore drill have been completed for floodway diversion routes of the Assiniboine river to lake Manitoba via both east and west of Portage la Prairie. Subsequent office study of this diversion

scheme is well advanced, and a design of floodways with appurtenant works is being carried out for flows of 10,000, 25,000 and
40,000	c.f.s. Preliminary estimates of quantities and costs are being derived.
This is a long statement. Shall I continue?

I do not
want to condemn the minister to reading a long report. I thought perhaps he could give us a summary. What interests me still more is whether the minister can summarize in a general way the investigation work which is going on, and most important just what decisions, if any, have been made as to what is to be done.

The surveys are still being carried out. We are still doing some drilling on various parts of the rivers to determine the type of bottoms and various other findings that are required to determine the whole structure of the countryside with which we are concerned. Most of the field work has now been done. It is being compiled in the form of engineering data and office studies. We are hopeful that a report will be available by the end of this year. That was the target date established when the survey was undertaken, and we are still hoping that this date will be possible of attainment.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
This whole subject out there is not a matter that can be dealt with briefly, or brought into a very small report. In the first place, we have had the experience arising out of the Winnipeg flood of 1948 and the undertakings that followed as a means of protecting the city of Winnipeg. May I say to the committee that the recurring serious flood problem of Manitoba has not been on the Red river but rather on the Assiniboine river, and more particularly from the area in the neighbourhood of Portage la Prairie east. Here we have had continually in regular recurring years a rather serious flood problem. And if I may say so to those associated with the city of Winnipeg, flood protection actions which they may have taken there I am sure result in aggravating the situation that happens to exist on the Assiniboine river. It cannot be otherwise.
I noted that the minister made reference to surveys that were undertaken in the area of Portage la Prairie last year, I understood at the instigation of the international joint commission, with the work being carried out by the prairie farm rehabilitation organization. We all know that these surveys were carried on, and we are anxiously awaiting their reports.
1952
Supply-Resources and Development I might say to the minister and the committee that any undertaking to divert the Assiniboine river under flood conditions across to lake Manitoba is going to cost a tremendous lot of money, more than might ordinarily be expected because of the type of soil. It is a highly alluvial soil and moves around almost like feathers. Therefore whether or not it would stand any flow of water going through it is not only questionable but quite problematical.
In addition to that, the project would require going across three railways on the trans-Canada highway besides bridging other routes and things of that character. On the other hand the Assiniboine river, as those of us who live along it know, has been a problem, largely owing to flood conditions, for upwards of 25 years. An average of probably $10,000 a year has been spent in trying to control the flooding along that river. Perhaps some of that money has not been spent to the best of advantage through having to be utilized to build dikes at bends in the river where the water was likely to overflow. But as time went on and erosion took place these river banks have washed away and the dikes have fallen in. Consequently much of that effort has been lost.
We-and when I say "we" I mean the people interested1-have been attempting to follow in later times a different program, namely that of trying to straighten out some of the very severe crooks that occur in that river. It is a very winding river. We think if we can get the water away more quickly from the mouth of the river, then it will avoid much of the flooding further back; but of course that then aggravates, if you like, the situation in the city of Winnipeg in that it brings the water down more quickly, and it in turn brings about another very serious problem there. But I think this whole project, both for the Red river and the Assiniboine river, involves a much wider program, through additional flood protection on the Assiniboine river, through straightening the bends and building certain dikes, and also probably the installation of storage dams further down the stream to hold back the overflow.
I hope the minister will be able to have this report on the prospects of diverting the river across to lake Manitoba at Portage la Prairie within a reasonable length of time, but I should like to suggest to him and to this committee that this is not in any sense a small undertaking. It involves a very large project and combines the flooding of the Red river as well as the Assiniboine river, and it must be approached in that light.

Supply-Resources and Development
I should like to express my interest in the report made by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa. Those of us who have listened to him feel that he should speak in this house much more often.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You would never get those estimates through, then.

Some of
the rest of us might not talk so much. With respect to the responsibility, I say again that the immediate responsibility assigned to the Department of Resources and Development was to conduct a survey with a view to determining what steps might be taken to reduce the hazard of flooding in the greater Winnipeg area. Once we have completed the surveys and prepared the report we will then certainly discuss with all parties concerned what the next steps should be.

But until that is available to us we must keep in mind our immediate objective, and that is to complete the surveys and compile the report.

I must content myself with the fact that the matter is being dealt with by someone much better informed, and leave it at that. I am glad to hear the minister say that he has noted what seemed to me to be the practical and immediate considerations put forward by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I wish to urge one thing more in connection with this. As I intimated before, this is a very big undertaking. Should the proposal to divert the Assiniboine river be undertaken seriously I should like to have the assurance from whatever authority may be dealing with it that there would be ample opportunity for those affected to express their points of view. I take from the minister's earlier statement that all his department has been doing thus far has been to arrange for surveys and to collect necessary information; and after that has been completed I understand somebody will have to determine the policy or make the recommendations as to which policy may be followed.
That is the point at which I think we must recognize and understand how the policy followed may affect individuals. I should not like to see anything go out from this committee as a result of the discussion which has taken place that would not assure those whose property may be affected that they will have ample opportunity to know what the project is going to be, how it is going to affect them, and what is involved so far as they are concerned.
I can assure the committee that the people living in the area immediately north of Portage la Prairie, out toward the lake, are vitally concerned in -the matter, and I am afraid they just would not accept kindly any thought that a project of this kind was going to be undertaken without their having full opportunity -to express their points of view and -to have them considered.

I understood the minister to say that the full responsibility of his department was to have a report ready by the end of the year. That leads me to ask where the responsibility lies, because after all something more than the preparation of a report must be done. Whose responsibility will it be to act in this matter? We will reach the end of -the year and come within easy range of the flood season before anything is done. Whose responsibility will it be?

When the report is prepared will the matter be allowed t.o rest without action?

The hon. member need have no fear in that connection. Once the report has been prepared it will be a matter of study by those concerned, both individually and in governments. As I have informed hon. members, we have been in close consultation with the government of Manitoba and will continue to be in close consultation with it. The city of Winnipeg must have consideration, too. I can assure all hon. members that once the report is available no time will be lost in bringing it to the at.ention of those concerned to see that they are given ample opportunity to study it. The decision can then be made as to what the next steps should be.

speechtext:
I had thought my observations were to the point. I am sorry if I have created the impression that I have been digressing from the item under discussion. Supply-Resources and Development control of the flood waters on that river. I was about to suggest that that is one problem which will have to be faced in any overall policy adopted in an attempt to control the flood waters not only of the Assiniboine but also of the Red river.

P.F.R.A. is already doing some of the survey work which will be used in the consolidation of the report. In effect they are doing it for the Department of Resources and Development. 390.	Administration, $38,238.

I understand a delegation saw the minister some time ago with regard to the Conestogo project on the upper reaches of the Grand river. I know the minister must realize how serious the situation is on this river, and it is becoming even more serious. The losses from floods in the spring can be tremendous. I am sure the Ontario government has given permission to go ahead with this project, and I hope the dominion government is ready to contribute its share. Has anything definite been done so far regarding this matter?

A delegation came to see me and requested the federal government to contribute to the construction of the Conestogo dam on the Grand river. This delegation came through the good offices of His Honour the Speaker, and we had a full and pleasant interview. I told them that whether or not
IMr. Brooks.]

the federal government participated would be dependent upon the project being considered to be in the national interest. Quite apart from the dam the provincial government would have the onus of convincing the federal government that there were other features involved, such as forest and soil conservation, which would make this project of national interest. In other words it would have to be the sort of project toward which all taxpayers would feel justified in contributing. The delegation undertook to look into the problem on that broader basis. I believe they have written since that time and the department is studying their submission.
Is the minister saying that flood conditions are not a problem of the dominion government?

As has been said here so often, flood conditions in the first instance are the responsibility of the municipality. If the damage is beyond the financial capacity of the municipality, it looks to the provincial government for assistance. If the problem created by the flood is considered to be so broad in character as to be beyond the fiscal capacity of the province and such as to merit participation by the taxpayers of Canada as a whole, then the federal government participates. That is the normal approach to problems of that nature.

I realized that there were a number of strings attached, but I did not think they went that far. The damage caused each year is almost equal to what it would cost to complete this Conestogo project. Great flood damage is caused in Brantford and Paris. I am more particularly interested in the latter municipality where the river runs right through the town and the damage can be considerable. In a few years the amount of damage would more than equal the cost of the dam. I hope the minister will consider this matter beyond the national aspect of conservation.

Do I understand the
minister to say that flood damage on such great rivers as the St. Lawrence and Fraser is the responsibility of the municipality?

If a municipality suffers damage, the responsibility in the first instance lies with the municipality. If the damage is of such magnitude as occurred in the case of the Fraser and Red rivers it becomes beyond the capacity of the municipality. In those instances it was considered to be beyond the capacity of the provincial governments and therefore it involved the interests of the taxpayers of Canada as represented by the federal government.	*

Conditions have changed considerably since early days. Today we have the Canadian National Railways and millions of dollars of federal money invested in national projects. Surely the minister is not going to tell me that the responsibility would rest with a little municipality having a revenue of no more than $200,000 or $300,000. I do not deprecate what the federal government did in the case of the Red and Fraser rivers at the time of our national disasters, but it seems strange to me to hear the minister say that in the case of these great rivers-I am speaking only for the Fraser, as I know very little about the Red river-the responsibility would be that of the local municipality in the case of flood.
In the first instance it is. Whether or not they are required to bear the full responsibility is another matter. That depends entirely upon the magnitude of the disaster.

I want to follow that up a little. I am only speaking about the river I know something about, and right at the present time it happens to be our danger period in British Columbia. Under the act as it now stands does your department not have the right to vote funds to protect your investment? What I am trying to get at is that the local municipality could not possibly do it, and I am asking the question for purposes of information. Under your department have you not the right now to vote moneys to protect the investment, if you like to put it that way, that you have at the present time in protection from flood damage in such rivers as the Fraser?

Furthermore, I notice there is a large increase in this item. A survey has been going on at Rustico harbour over to Robinsons island, with a view to building a bridge there and connecting the Rustico-Cavendish part of the national park with Dalvay and the eastern part. I have not seen any report as to whether this survey is going to be continued this year or, furthermore, whether a bridge is going to be built across the harbour at Rustico. This is one of the projects that was up for consideration prior to 1949. Having regard to the size of this vote as compared with that of other years,
I should like to know whether this highway


is going to be completed. Another question I should like to ask is this. Are any negotiations in progress with the provincial government with regard to the building of a highway from New Glasgow, Prince Edward Island to Cavendish. It is only a distance of six miles. Some preparation has already been made by the provincial government with regard to the road. In visiting Cavendish, one drawback is this six miles of dirt road which could be made into a satisfactory highway. I understand the provincial government are ready to pay their share if the federal government will come in and assist in making it a permanent highway to connect with the highway at New Glasgow; they will then have a perfect road right through and get clear of all the dust about which there are so many complaints at the present time.
I know it is after eleven o'clock. The minister will take quite a while to reply to this question-
It will not take me very long to reply.
We had better have the question left over.

None of the projects to which my hon. friend the senior member for Queens referred comes within the scope of this vote. None of them is on the route of the trans-Canada highway. He was discussing certain contemplated projects in the national park. All I can tell him is that we propose this year to complete the paving of that portion of the roadway between Dalvay and Stanhope. The other projects are outside the scope of this vote.
Eleven o'clock.
